claim: Dopamine neurons fired more strongly to unpredicted than to predicted reward.
source: This proposal was initially based on observations that these neurons fired more strongly to unpredicted than to predicted reward, suppressed firing on omission of a predicted reward, and developed firing to reward-paired cues with learning (Mirenowicz and Schultz, 1994).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Mirenowicz and Schultz, 1994.

claim: Dopamine neurons suppressed firing on omission of a predicted reward.
source: This proposal was initially based on observations that these neurons fired more strongly to unpredicted than to predicted reward, suppressed firing on omission of a predicted reward, and developed firing to reward-paired cues with learning (Mirenowicz and Schultz, 1994).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Mirenowicz and Schultz, 1994.

claim: Dopamine neurons developed firing to reward-paired cues with learning.
source: This proposal was initially based on observations that these neurons fired more strongly to unpredicted than to predicted reward, suppressed firing on omission of a predicted reward, and developed firing to reward-paired cues with learning (Mirenowicz and Schultz, 1994).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Mirenowicz and Schultz, 1994.

claim: Phasic activity in dopamine neurons obeys formal predictions for TD error signals under complex conditions.
source: Further work has shown that phasic activity in dopamine neurons obeys formal predictions for such TD error signals under more complex conditions (Waelti et al., 2001; Tobler et al., 2003; Lak et al., 2014; Pan et al., 2005; Hart et al., 2014; Bayer and Glimcher, 2005; Hollerman and Schultz, 1998), including in tasks such as blocking and conditioned inhibition, in which experimental conditions are arranged to precisely distinguish between prediction error signals and other possible explanations of such activity.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to studies demonstrating this phenomenon.

claim: The activity of dopamine neurons provides a quantitative match with the error signal described in the TD model.
source: Indeed careful work in monkeys has shown that the activity provides a quantitative match with the error signal described in the TD model (Bayer and Glimcher, 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Bayer and Glimcher, 2005.

claim: Artificially stimulating or inhibiting likely dopamine neurons for very brief periods is sufficient to restore the associative learning driven by endogenous positive or negative prediction errors in rats.
source: With the advent of optogenetic techniques and Cre-driver lines in rats, it has also been shown in rats that artificially stimulating or inhibiting likely dopamine neurons for very brief periods is sufficient to restore the associative learning driven by endogenous positive or negative prediction errors (Steinberg et al., 2013; Chang et al., 2016), suggesting that phasic activity in dopamine neurons can act like a prediction error, at least in some downstream targets and behavioral paradigms (Glimcher, 2011; Schultz, 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Steinberg et al., 2013 and Chang et al., 2016.

claim: Phasic activity in dopamine neurons can act like a prediction error, at least in some downstream targets and behavioral paradigms.
source: With the advent of optogenetic techniques and Cre-driver lines in rats, it has also been shown in rats that artificially stimulating or inhibiting likely dopamine neurons for very brief periods is sufficient to restore the associative learning driven by endogenous positive or negative prediction errors (Steinberg et al., 2013; Chang et al., 2016), suggesting that phasic activity in dopamine neurons can act like a prediction error, at least in some downstream targets and behavioral paradigms (Glimcher, 2011; Schultz, 2002).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the optogenetic studies and supported by citations to Glimcher, 2011 and Schultz, 2002.

claim: The errors in TD models are based on the value that has been assigned to events based on direct experience.
source: The errors in TD models, at least as they have been applied to interpret the firing of dopamine neurons, are based on the value that has been assigned to events based on direct experience (Glimcher, 2011; Schultz, 2002; Niv and Schoenbaum, 2008; Clark et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations describing TD models.

claim: Cached value is pre-computed and resides in the predictive event.
source: This so-called cached value is pre-computed and resides in the predictive event, be it a primary reward or reward-predicting cue.
evidence: This is a definitional statement about cached value in TD models, drawing from established knowledge.

claim: The value in TD models is calculated free of any other predictive information about the environment, defining this class of algorithms as model-free.
source: The value is calculated free of any other predictive information about the environment, defining this class of algorithms as model-free.
evidence: This is a definitional statement about model-free algorithms, drawing from established knowledge.

claim: TD models are unable to compute prediction errors elicited in situations in which value is derived through inference rather than through direct experience.
source: While these TD models have been extremely powerful in interpreting the activity of dopamine neurons in tasks in which value is based on experienced reward, they are unable to compute prediction errors elicited in situations in which value is derived through inference rather than through direct experience.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the limitations of TD models based on their definition as model-free.

claim: Deriving a value based on inference is a hallmark of model-based algorithms.
source: Deriving a value (or a prediction) based on inference – meaning to deduce from an understanding of the relationships amongst environmental stimuli and events - is a hallmark of a second class of algorithms, termed model-based (Daw et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Daw et al., 2005.

claim: Much of our real world behavior is based on model-based inference.
source: This distinction between algorithms is important because much of our real world behavior, and thus many of our opportunities for error-driven learning, is based on this model-based inference (Daw et al., 2005; Doll et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Daw et al., 2005 and Doll et al., 2012.

claim: In sensory pre-conditioning, animals first learn that one innocuous cue (cue A) predicts another (cue B), in the absence of reward, and then later learn that the second cue (B) is a reliable predictor of reward.
source: This basic concept is operationalized (and the effect of such inferred or model-based value, isolated) in sensory pre-conditioning (Brogden, 1939). In this task, animals first learn that one innocuous cue (cue A) predicts another (cue B), in the absence of reward, and then later learn that the second cue (B) is a reliable predictor of reward.
evidence: This is a description of the sensory pre-conditioning paradigm, supported by citation to Brogden, 1939.

claim: Cue A in sensory pre-conditioning has not been directly paired with reward and thus has not had any opportunity to acquire any cached value.
source: Cue A has not been directly paired with reward and thus it has not had any opportunity to acquire any cached value (Glimcher, 2011; Niv and Schoenbaum, 2008).
evidence: This is a logical inference about cue A based on the experimental design, supported by citations.

claim: Cue A in sensory pre-conditioning cannot elicit a TD prediction error, despite having value as defined by the animal's responding and its ability to modulate error-driven learning.
source: As a result, cue A cannot elicit a TD prediction error, despite the fact that it has value as defined by the animal's responding and its ability to modulate error-driven learning (Jones et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a logical inference about TD models' inability to account for cue A's value, supported by citation to Jones et al., 2012.

claim: If TD models are an accurate and complete description of the information contained in dopamine neuron activity, then cue A should not elicit dopamine neuron firing above the level of a control cue.
source: If TD models are an accurate and complete description of the information contained in dopamine neuron activity, then cue A should not elicit dopamine neuron firing, at least not above the level of a control cue.
evidence: This is a logical prediction based on TD model assumptions.

claim: 14 rats were trained with recording electrodes implanted in the ventral tegmental area (VTA) in a sensory-preconditioning task.
source: To test this, we trained 14 rats with recording electrodes implanted in the ventral tegmental area (VTA) in a sensory-preconditioning task.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental design.

claim: In the first phase of training, rats learned to associate two pairs of environmental cues (A->B; C->D) in the absence of reward.
source: In the first phase, rats learned to associate two pairs of environmental cues (A->B; C->D) in the absence of reward.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental design.

claim: During the first phase of training, rats showed no significant responding at the food cup and no differences in responding during the different cues.
source: As there was no reward, rats showed no significant responding at the food cup and no differences in responding during the different cues (ANOVA, F3, 55 = 0.7, p=0.52; Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis (ANOVA) and reference to Figure 1A.

claim: In the second phase, rats learned that cue B predicted reward and cue D did not.
source: In the second phase, rats learned that the second cue of one pair (B) predicted reward and the other (D) did not; learning was reflected in an increase in responding at the food cup during presentation of B (ANOVA, main effect of cue: F 1, 163 = 280.1, p<0.001, main effect of session: F 5, 163 = 9.7, interaction: F 5, 163 = 10.81, p<0.001; Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis (ANOVA) and reference to Figure 1B.

claim: Learning in the second phase was reflected in an increase in responding at the food cup during presentation of B.
source: In the second phase, rats learned that the second cue of one pair (B) predicted reward and the other (D) did not; learning was reflected in an increase in responding at the food cup during presentation of B (ANOVA, main effect of cue: F 1, 163 = 280.1, p<0.001, main effect of session: F 5, 163 = 9.7, interaction: F 5, 163 = 10.81, p<0.001; Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis (ANOVA) and reference to Figure 1B.

claim: In the third phase, rats responded at the food cup significantly more during presentation of A than during presentation of C.
source: As expected, the rats responded at the food cup significantly more during presentation of A, the cue that predicted B, than during presentation of C, the cue that predicted D (ANOVA, main effect of cue: F 1, 167 = 8.7, p<0.001, main effect of trial: F 5, 167 = 6.08, p<0.001, interaction: F 5, 167 = 2.07, p=0.07; Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis (ANOVA) and reference to Figure 1C.

claim: Single unit activity was recorded in the VTA throughout training.
source: Single unit activity was recorded in the VTA throughout training.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental methods.

claim: An optogenetically-validated strategy classifies VTA neurons on the basis of their response dynamics during Pavlovian conditioning and identifies VTA dopamine neurons with near perfect fidelity.
source: To identify putative dopamine neurons, we used a recently developed, optogenetically-validated strategy that classifies VTA neurons on the basis of their response dynamics during Pavlovian conditioning. In published work (Cohen et al., 2012; Eshel et al., 2015), this strategy identified VTA dopamine neurons (i.e. neurons expressing Cre under the control of the promoter for the dopamine transporter) with near perfect fidelity.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Cohen et al., 2012 and Eshel et al., 2015.

claim: The classification analysis successfully extracted 3 previously described VTA response types: neurons with sustained excitation to cues and reward (putative GABAergic), neurons with phasic excitation to cue onset and reward onset (putative dopaminergic), and neurons with sustained inhibition to cue and reward (unknown).
source: This analysis successfully extracted the 3 previously described VTA response types from our data (Figure 2D): neurons with sustained excitation to cues and reward (putative GABAergic), neurons with phasic excitation to cue onset and reward onset (putative dopaminergic), and neurons with sustained inhibition to cue and reward (unknown).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data analysis and reference to Figure 2D.

claim: Putative dopamine neurons (n = 304) showed changes in firing during conditioning that were in accord with signaling of reward prediction errors.
source: We then assessed the responses of the putative dopamine neurons (n = 304) to the cue and reward over the course of conditioning. Consistent with their classification, we found changes in firing during conditioning that were in accord with signaling of reward prediction errors.
evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis of neural responses during conditioning.

claim: Early in conditioning, putative dopamine neurons' maximal response occurred just after reward delivery.
source: Specifically, early in conditioning, these neurons' maximal response occurred just after reward delivery (Figure 2E, top trace), whereas late in conditioning, the maximal response occurred just after onset of the cue predicting that reward (Figure 2E, lower traces).
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Figure 2E.

claim: Late in conditioning, putative dopamine neurons' maximal response occurred just after onset of the cue predicting reward.
source: Specifically, early in conditioning, these neurons' maximal response occurred just after reward delivery (Figure 2E, top trace), whereas late in conditioning, the maximal response occurred just after onset of the cue predicting that reward (Figure 2E, lower traces).
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Figure 2E.

claim: The difference in activity at the time of cue onset versus reward increased significantly from the start to the end of conditioning in putative dopamine neurons.
source: As a result, the difference in activity at the time of cue onset versus reward increased significantly from the start to the end of conditioning (r 302 = 0.24, p<0.01; Figure 2F), consistent with signaling of TD prediction errors (Glimcher, 2011; Schultz, 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis and reference to Figure 2F.

claim: The change in firing of putative dopamine neurons during conditioning is consistent with signaling of TD prediction errors.
source: As a result, the difference in activity at the time of cue onset versus reward increased significantly from the start to the end of conditioning (r 302 = 0.24, p<0.01; Figure 2F), consistent with signaling of TD prediction errors (Glimcher, 2011; Schultz, 2002).
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the data, supported by citations to Glimcher, 2011 and Schultz, 2002.

claim: 52 putative dopamine neurons were identified during the probe test by their pattern of firing to the reward predictive cue.
source: We again identified these neurons by their pattern of firing to the reward predictive cue (n = 102; Figure 3A–D). As before, this analysis identified a group of cells with strong phasic responses to B, the cue that had been directly paired with reward (n = 52).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the number of neurons identified, supported by reference to Figure 3A-D.

claim: Putative dopamine neurons fired significantly more during the first second of B than to D.
source: While this response generalized somewhat to D, the control cue that had been presented without reward during conditioning sessions, these neurons fired significantly more during the first second of B than to D (t 51 = 4.40, p<0.001, black versus gray lines, respectively, with shading for SEM, Figure 3E).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis (t-test) and reference to Figure 3E.

claim: Putative dopamine neurons exhibited the largest responses at the onset of B and to A.
source: While the classified putative dopamine neurons showed firing to all cues, they exhibited the largest responses at the onset of B, the reward-paired cue (significantly above responding to D, t (51) = 4.40, p<0.001), and to A, the cue that had been paired with B in the preconditioning phase (significantly above responding to control cue C, t (51) = 5.02, p<0.001) (E–F).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis and reference to Figure 3E-F.

claim: Putative dopamine neurons had strong phasic responses to both preconditioned cues A and C.
source: However, in addition to this expected pattern of firing, these cells also had strong phasic responses to both preconditioned cues (blue and red traces, A and C, respectively, with shading for SEM, Figure 3E).
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Figure 3E.

claim: The phasic neural response was significantly stronger for A than for C.
source: While the common element of these responses could reflect novelty or salience, since these cues had not been presented for a number of days, or perhaps generalization from conditioning to B, the actual phasic neural response was significantly stronger for A, the cue that predicted the reward-paired cue, than for C, the preconditioned control cue (t 51 = 5.02, p<0.001).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis (t-test).

claim: The difference in neural response between A and C cannot be explained on the basis of novelty, salience, or generalization, since A and C were treated similarly.
source: This difference cannot be explained on the basis of novelty, salience, or generalization, since A and C were treated similarly.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the experimental design.

claim: The difference in neural response between A and C cannot be explained by direct experience with reward, because A was never paired with reward, and it was only paired with B before conditioning.
source: Nor can it be explained by direct experience with reward, because A was never paired with reward, and it was only paired with B before conditioning.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the experimental design.

claim: The phasic response in putative dopamine neurons appeared to be influenced by inferred value of cue A.
source: Thus, the phasic response in these putative dopamine neurons appeared to be influenced by inferred value of cue A.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data based on the experimental design and results.

claim: The neural response was perhaps somewhat better at discriminating A from C than B from D.
source: Interestingly, the neural response was perhaps somewhat better at discriminating A from C (Figure 3E, bottom panel) than B from D (Figure 3E, top panel), perhaps reflecting the differences in training between A and C, which were only presented a few times in unrewarded sessions, versus B and D, which were presented many times across several days of conditioning.
evidence: This is an observation from the data with a speculative explanation.

claim: The influence of the inferred value of cue A on the firing of putative dopamine neurons during the first second of their cue response was strongly and significantly correlated with the influence of value on these neurons firing at the onset of B.
source: Despite this, the influence of the inferred value of cue A on the firing of these neurons during the first second of their cue response was strongly and significantly correlated with the influence of value on these neurons firing at the onset of B, the cue directly paired with reward (r 50 = 0.63, p<0.001; Figure 3F).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis (correlation) and reference to Figure 3F.

claim: The correlation between responses to A and B was also true for 4 neurons that exhibited the classic wide, polyphasic waveforms traditionally used to identify dopamine neurons.
source: Notably this was also true for a handful of neurons (n = 4) that exhibited the classic wide, polyphasic waveforms traditionally used to identify dopamine neurons (Figure 3F, filled circles, see Figure 3—figure supplement 1 for PSTH's).
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Figure 3F and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The relationship in the initial phasic response to the cues did not reach significance in the other two neural subtypes identified by the clustering analysis.
source: This relationship in the initial phasic response to the cues did not reach significance in the other two neural subtypes identified by the clustering analysis (see Figure 3—figure supplements 2 and 3 for analyses of tonically-modulated neurons).
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Figure 3—figure supplements 2 and 3.

claim: The average response of putative dopamine neurons throughout cues A and C was above baseline, and this sustained firing was significantly higher to cue A than C.
source: Beyond their phasic responses at the start of the cues and to reward, the putative dopamine neurons also exhibited another notable feature: the average response of these neurons throughout cues A and C was above baseline, and this sustained firing was significantly higher to cue A than C (Figure 3E, final 9s of cues, t51 = 2.56, p<0.05).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis (t-test) and reference to Figure 3E.

claim: The elevated sustained firing during cue A may be a sign of dopamine's reported ability to anticipate proximity to reward or to signal state value.
source: This elevated firing may be a sign of dopamine's reported ability to anticipate proximity to reward or to signal state value (Howe et al., 2013; Hamid et al., 2016), if our rats' expectation of reward delivery is based on knowing that progression to the offset of cue A should lead to the subsequent presentation of cue B and then reward.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the data, supported by citations to Howe et al., 2013 and Hamid et al., 2016.

claim: The pattern of sustained firing is not present throughout cue B.
source: Importantly, in our design, reward is presented during B rather than at its termination. This would explain why this pattern of sustained firing is not present throughout cue B (Figure 3E, t51= 1.09, p=0.278).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis (t-test) and reference to Figure 3E.

claim: The pattern of sustained and differential firing to A (vs C) and not to B (vs D) in the putative dopamine neurons is the mirror image of firing in neurons classified as tonically excited.
source: Interestingly this pattern of sustained and differential firing to A (vs C) and not to B (vs D) in the putative dopamine neurons is the mirror image of firing in neurons classified as tonically excited, which showed relatively modest changes in sustained firing to A and C and much larger increases in firing to B (see Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Tonically excited neurons are thought to be GABAergic.
source: This relationship would be consistent with recent proposals that these neurons, thought to be GABAergic (Cohen et al., 2012), exert tonic inhibition to suppress the firing of dopamine neurons (Eshel et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Cohen et al., 2012 and Eshel et al., 2015.

claim: Tonically excited neurons exert tonic inhibition to suppress the firing of dopamine neurons.
source: This relationship would be consistent with recent proposals that these neurons, thought to be GABAergic (Cohen et al., 2012), exert tonic inhibition to suppress the firing of dopamine neurons (Eshel et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Eshel et al., 2015.

claim: VTA dopamine neurons exhibited phasic cue-evoked responses that were influenced by inferred value.
source: Here we report that VTA dopamine neurons, identified based either on traditional waveform criteria or through an optogenetically-validated clustering analysis of their response properties to a conditioned cue, exhibited phasic cue-evoked responses that were influenced by inferred value.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the main finding, supported by the data presented.

claim: The phasic responses to cue A were observed even though the critical cue had no prior history of direct pairing with any rewarding event.
source: These responses were observed even though the critical cue had no prior history of direct pairing with any rewarding event.
evidence: This is a statement about the experimental design.

claim: The phasic responses to cue A were greater than responses to a control cue that was treated similarly and thus had similar levels of salience or novelty or generalized value.
source: In addition, they were greater than responses to a control cue that was treated similarly and thus had similar levels of salience or novelty or generalized value, all variables that have been proposed to explain phasic activity in other settings that appeared to be at odds with the standard explanation of phasic dopamine activity (Kakade and Dayan, 2002; Bromberg-Martin et al., 2010; Matsumoto and Hikosaka, 2009).
evidence: This is a statement about the data and its interpretation, supported by citations.

claim: The phasic activity of dopamine neurons can reflect information about value that is not contemplated by TD models.
source: These data show that the phasic activity of dopamine neurons can reflect information about value that is not contemplated by TD models, at least as they have been applied to understand the phasic firing of these neurons (Glimcher, 2011; Schultz, 2002; Niv and Schoenbaum, 2008; Clark et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data, supported by citations.

claim: The finding is consistent with recent reports suggesting that dopamine neurons are likely to access more complex information than is available to standard TD models.
source: Our finding is consistent with a number of recent reports, suggesting that dopamine neurons are likely to access more complex information than is available to standard TD models.
evidence: This is a statement placing the findings in context with other research.

claim: Dopamine neurons in the rat VTA utilize input from the orbitofrontal cortex to disambiguate states that are not easily distinguished via external information in order to more accurately calculate prediction errors.
source: For example, dopamine neurons in the rat VTA utilize input from the orbitofrontal cortex to disambiguate states that are not easily distinguished via external information in order to more accurately calculate prediction errors (Takahashi et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Takahashi et al., 2011.

claim: Dopamine neurons have access to a major source of state information, given the central role of the orbitofrontal cortex in inference-based behavior.
source: While this result does not require the use of inference in calculating errors, merely access to state information, it suggests that dopamine neurons have access to a major source of this information, given the central role of the orbitofrontal cortex in inference-based behavior (Stalnaker et al., 2015).
evidence: This is an inference based on the role of OFC, supported by citation to Stalnaker et al., 2015.

claim: The phasic activity of dopamine neurons has been shown to track the value of one cue after changes in the value of an associated cue.
source: The phasic activity of dopamine neurons has also been shown to track the value of one cue after changes in the value of an associated cue (Bromberg-Martin et al., 2010b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Bromberg-Martin et al., 2010b.

claim: The inference seen in the Bromberg-Martin et al. task may differ from that shown in the current study in that it does not require access to model-based information, but could instead be based on direct, 'cached' value from earlier training sessions.
source: Indeed these authors describe their results in terms of inference; however, as they note in their discussion (Bromberg-Martin et al., 2010b, final paragraph of discussion), the inference seen in their task may differ from that shown here in that it does not require access to model-based information, but could instead be based on direct, 'cached' value from earlier training sessions.
evidence: This is a critical analysis of another study, supported by citation to Bromberg-Martin et al., 2010b.

claim: Elevated dopamine has been found using microdialysis during an aversive version of the sensory preconditioning task.
source: Finally elevated dopamine has also been found using microdialysis during an aversive version of the sensory preconditioning task used here (Young et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Young et al., 1998.

claim: The use of an aversive paradigm, a measurement technique with low temporal resolution, and the lack of control conditions in the Young et al. study make it difficult to apply these results to address the proposal that phasic changes in the firing of dopamine neurons signal TD prediction errors in appetitive paradigms.
source: However the use of an aversive paradigm, a measurement technique with low temporal resolution, and the lack of control conditions to confirm signaling of cached value errors make it difficult to apply these results to address the very specific proposal that phasic changes in the firing of dopamine neurons signal TD prediction errors in appetitive paradigms.
evidence: This is a critical analysis of the limitations of another study.

claim: The current study records phasic activity of dopamine neurons at their source.
source: Our study addresses the limitations of these best available prior reports. We are recording phasic activity of dopamine neurons at their source.
evidence: This is a statement about the experimental methods.

claim: Dopamine neurons were identified by two different classification schemes: waveform criteria and an optogenetically-validated clustering approach.
source: We have identified dopamine neurons by two different classification schemes, an old one that has been used repeatedly across labs and species to identify error-signaling dopamine neurons (Mirenowicz and Schultz, 1994; Waelti et al., 2001; Tobler et al., 2003; Pan et al., 2005; Roesch et al., 2007; Jo et al., 2013; Morris et al., 2006; Jin and Costa, 2010), as well as a new, optogenetically-validated approach that has identified error signals in mice (Cohen et al., 2012) and is favored by those that dislike the use of waveform criteria (Margolis et al., 2006).
evidence: This is a statement about the experimental methods, supported by multiple citations.

claim: The critical cue of interest (cue A) has no prior history of association with reward, thus unique firing to this cue cannot be explained as any sort of cached value.
source: We used a carefully designed behavioral preparation in which our critical cue of interest has no prior history of association with reward, thus unique firing to this cue cannot be explained as any sort of cached value (see 'A comment on the basis of responding to the preconditioned cue' in the behavioral Methods for further information).
evidence: This is a statement about the experimental design and its implications.

claim: The appetitive task includes two important control cues: one designed to rule out explanations based on generalization and salience (cue C) and another designed to reveal cached value prediction errors (cue B).
source: Further this appetitive task includes two important control cues: one designed to rule out explanations based on generalization and salience (cue C) and another designed to reveal cached value prediction errors (cue B).
evidence: This is a statement about the experimental design.

claim: The inclusion of cue B is important because it allows assessment of the relationship between traditional error signals and any influence of inferred value on the firing of the dopamine neurons.
source: The inclusion of this cue in particular is important because it allows us to assess the relationship between traditional error signals and any influence of inferred value on the firing of the dopamine neurons.
evidence: This is a statement about the experimental design and its rationale.

claim: The close relationship in the firing of the dopamine neurons to B and A suggests that whatever is ultimately signaled when a cue with inferred, model based value is presented may be similar to what the same neurons signal in response to the unexpected appearance of a cue that has been directly paired with reward.
source: The close relationship in the firing of the dopamine neurons to B, the cue directly paired with reward, and A, the cue that predicts reward only through B, suggests that whatever is ultimately signaled when a cue with inferred, model based value is presented may be similar to what the same neurons signal in response to the unexpected appearance of a cue that has been directly paired with reward.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data.

claim: Inferred and experienced value are confounded for a cue directly paired with reward, as illustrated by the normal efficacy of reinforcer devaluation at changing conditioned responding.
source: While this might be explained as error signaling to B, calculated from TD models, and error signaling to A, calculated from something beyond TD models, this solution is cumbersome, particularly given that inferred and experienced value are actually confounded for a cue directly paired with reward (a fact illustrated by the normal efficacy of reinforcer devaluation at changing conditioned responding [Holland and Straub, 1979]).
evidence: This is a logical argument supported by citation to Holland and Straub, 1979.

claim: A more parsimonious explanation is that dopamine neurons have access to a wide variety of information when computing expected value.
source: A more parsimonious explanation is that dopamine neurons, unlike standard TD models, have access to a wide variety of information when computing expected value.
evidence: This is a proposed interpretation of the findings.

claim: While dopamine neuron firing may conform to what is expected for errors calculated from TD models in some special cases, they may not be signaling TD derived errors.
source: And that while their firing may conform to what is expected for errors calculated from TD models in some special cases, they may not be signaling TD derived errors.
evidence: This is a proposed interpretation of the findings.

claim: The suggestion that dopamine neurons access a wide variety of information aligns with recent proposals that dopamine neurons signal errors based on changes in economic utility.
source: Such a suggestion aligns nicely with recent proposals that dopamine neurons signal errors based on changes in economic utility (Schultz et al., 2015), and it would be consistent with data presented in abstract form suggesting that cue-evoked dopamine release in nucleus accumbens is sensitive to devaluation of a paired reward (Martinez et al., 2008), though it contradicts data only just published from a similar study in which cue-evoked release was not immediately altered when reward value was manipulated via salt depletion (Cone et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a statement placing the findings in context with other research, supported by citations.

claim: The variability in correspondence between unit data and evidence from studies of dopamine efflux in accumbens may reflect the different dynamics of the two processes or may indicate some specificity with regard to the information content of the dopaminergic afferents in accumbens versus other areas.
source: This variability in correspondence between our unit data and evidence from studies of dopamine efflux in accumbens may reflect to the different dynamics of the two processes or it may indicate some specificity with regard to the information content of the dopaminergic afferents in accumbens versus other areas.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for discrepancies in the literature.

claim: The general proposal that phasic changes in dopamine are a TD error signal incorporates two very separate sets of predictions: one concerning the information used to construct the error signals, and another concerning what the dopaminergic errors do downstream.
source: Finally it is important to explicitly note that the general proposal that phasic changes in dopamine are a TD error signal incorporates two very separate sets of predictions. One set, most relevant to the single unit correlates that form the basis of this hypothesis, concerns the information used to construct the error signals. This is obviously the part of the question we have addressed in the current study. That is, do dopaminergic errors reflect only model-free information derived from TD systems or do they also incorporate the predictions of non-TD, model-based systems? We believe our data favor the latter position. The second set of predictions, not addressed by our study, concerns what the dopaminergic errors do downstream.
evidence: This is a conceptual clarification about the implications of the study.
